extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of natural history, taxonomy, and philosophy of science; naturalists and scientists interested in principles of classification and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and principles for constructing and evaluating classifications (genera, species, orders) and for understanding limits of scientific method and laws of nature in the natural sciences. Emphasises practical rules, logical pitfalls, and the probabilistic nature of laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latitude in definitions of natural orders
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow considerable latitude in the definition of natural orders when a very strict definition either includes too many forms or produces anomalous genera that do not conform in all respects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a family is defined too broadly it will include disparate forms; if too narrow it creates anomalous genera. Example: Cruciferae described as having pods divided into two cells, yet some genera have one-celled or indehiscent pods — this forces either loosened family definition or recognition of closely associated families.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid strict typological classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not treat the type (an individual) as if other objects could exactly resemble it; classification by types is logically erroneous unless individual peculiarities are abstracted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One must abstract a finite number of qualities from the type to constitute a class; otherwise the method leads to inconsistent or overlapping classes. The 'type' is an individual, and classes arise by specifying shared qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise gradation and hereditary descent
rubrics_metrics.description: Accept that gradation of characters (continuous variation) is probably the rule under hereditary descent and that precise demarcation between groups is the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge that many forms admit of intermediate links; rigid logical demarcations may be inappropriate. The remedy for classificatory laxity is frank recognition of gradation rather than forcing sharp boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species and genera as practical/arbitrary constructs
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat species and genera as classes created by the naturalist's mind according to degrees of resemblance, not as eternally fixed creations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All resemblances are natural insofar as they express hereditary affinities; distinctions between varieties, subspecies, species, and genera are matters of degree and often arbitrary. Historical doctrines that tied species to distinct creations are inadequate for modern classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: No rigorous universal criterion for species/genus difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not expect a single rigorous, universally applicable criterion to separate species from genera; the amount of structural peculiarity distinguishing genus from species cannot be precisely defined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempts to establish strict criteria have been fruitless; classifications must allow for continuous degrees of structural peculiarity and cannot rely on an absolute yardstick.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use but do not invert formal taxonomic ranks
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt the set of taxonomic ranks (kingdom, division, class, order, tribe, genus, species, variety, etc.) but respect the fixed order of successive sub-divisions and avoid inverting ranks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Botanical Nomenclature (e.g., 1867 Congress) recognises many ranks (up to twenty-one) and allows variation in attributed rank importance, but inversion of the arrangement (e.g., dividing a genus into orders) is inadmissible. The list is extensible and rank importance can vary by opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect and handle unique/nondescript objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipate unique or sui generis objects that stand apart with few analogies and treat them as nondescript or effectively forming a genus by themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unique objects (e.g., the rings of Saturn, carbon as a uniquely compound-forming element) require special treatment and may highlight boundaries or breakdowns in previous classificatory distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply law of continuity to apparent exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempt to find intermediate links between extreme or exceptional cases and ordinary cases, since many apparent anomalies are connected by intermediate instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comparative investigation to show continuity (e.g., regeneration of limbs across taxa is gradational). The presence of intermediate cases often converts apparent anomalies into part of a generalised series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyse mixtures quantitatively for accurate classification
rubrics_metrics.description: When phenomena are mixtures or aggregates (mixed light, complex sounds, granites), precise classification requires analysis and measurement of the constituent components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Mixed light needs spectroscopic analysis and intensity measurement of each homogeneous ray; sound timbre requires decomposition into constituent pitches/intensities (Helmholtz's work); granite classification needs chemical or microscopic analysis of proportions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise limits where classification is impractical
rubrics_metrics.description: Accept that some domains (tastes, odours, emotions, faces, melodies, human character) vary by insensible degrees or are complex aggregates, making rigorous logical classification hopeless or currently impractical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For such phenomena, only rough groupings may be possible; finer discrimination may exceed present methods and may require new analytical techniques or may be inherently gradational without sharp boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification's purpose: detect resemblances and points of difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification must detect resemblances of all degrees and ascertain exactly how far such resemblances extend, while assigning precisely the points at which difference begins, enabling valid inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification enables generalisation and inference; detecting differences prevents unjustified inference. A full classification is regarded as a complete record of our knowledge of the objects classified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of scientific method tied to limits of classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise that science can extend only as far as accurate classification goes; the limits of exact knowledge coincide with the limits of classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If resemblances cannot be detected and their exact character assigned, the inductive inferences that constitute science are not possible. Complexities may outpace scientific method's ability to classify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not include unascertainable elements in definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid defining classes or laws by elements that cannot possibly be ascertained (e.g., an act of creation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions should be based on observable characters; Darwin's admonition: 'the definition must not include an element which cannot possibly be ascertained.' Historical metaphysical concepts should not be used as classificatory criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat laws of nature as observed uniformities with probabilistic certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret laws of nature as general propositions about correlations observed to hold among bodies hitherto observed, always accompanied by an estimate of observed instances and a probability (less than certainty) that the law will hold in the next case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific laws are not necessary truths; inductive inferences always carry a non-zero probability of error. With every law we ought to join an estimate of the number of instances observed and the calculated probability that it will hold for future instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow for conceivable exceptions and alternative laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain logical openness to the discovery of exceptions or entirely different laws; the possibility of other laws is not incompatible with scientific method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: investigations of imaginary laws (Airy on perpetual motion; Laplace and Newton on alternative force laws). It would not be a reproach to scientific method to find exceptions (e.g., gravity without inertia) if observed; the method can accommodate such discoveries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dogmatic metaphysical extrapolation from scientific success
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not infer metaphysical conclusions (e.g., inevitable materialism, denial of free will, impossibility of Providence) solely from the success of particular scientific laws and methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific uniformities concern observed material agents and cannot logically prove that all other agents behave similarly. Over-exclusive study of physical sciences can generate overconfident, dogmatic spirit; one should be cautious about drawing theological or ultimate philosophical conclusions from inductive science.
